newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus leader defends detention of Russia TV crew.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader defends detention of Russia TV crew.

text.p: Belarussian leader Alexander Lukashenko, speaking in defence of the detention of a Russian television crew by his security service, accused the Russian media on Monday of waging an information war against him.
"The patience of both authorities and the people has its limits," Lukashenko said in the Belarussian capital Minsk. His remarks were broadcast by Russia's NTV commercial television.

"We have allowed too much (freedom) to foreign representations and the mass media. Other foreign media, such as those from Germany or the United States, do not dare to wage such information war against our people as the Russian media."
Lukashenko, who is forging closer ties with Russia, is seen in the West and by Russian liberals in and outside the government as increasingly authoritarian.

A crew of Russian Public Television (ORT) in Minsk, headed by Pavel Sheremet, was detained late on Saturday for what the authorities called illegal filming at a closed part of the Belarus-Lithuanian border.
NTV said they were being held in a KGB prison in the Western town of Grodno.
Belarus border guards' chief Alexander Pavlovsky said on Sunday that Sheremet's actions were punishable under the former Soviet republic's criminal code.
"Pavel Sheremet may get up to five years in prison under article 81 which includes punishment for illegal crossing of the border," Pavlovsky said.
It was not clear if Sheremet has been formally charged.

Sheremet was accused by the Belarussian authorities of biased reporting earlier this month and stripped of his foreign ministry media accreditation. Earlier this year, Belarus expelled a reporter for Russia's NTV television.

Lukashenko, who has been criticised in the West for his crackdown on the opposition, has closed some Belarussian newspapers down and ousted the editors of others. Some opposition newspapers are now published in Lithuania.
Russia's Foreign Ministry issued a guarded statement on Monday.
"The Foreign Ministry has repeatedly stated that it is concerned and worried over violations of journalists' rights," said the document, quoted by Itar-Tass news agency.
"At the same time there is a widely accepted principle that foreign journalists must strictly observe the laws and regulations of the country where they work."

Lukashenko rewrote the constitution in November last year after a landslide win at a referendum which critics said was illegitimate and ignored the old constitution. The new basic law gives him vast powers.

He has since signed a charter on a lose union between his country of 10 million and the 150 million-strong Russia but it was watered down by liberals in Moscow who feared it would give him too much a say in Russia's policy.
